<meta>continues from previous page: the plumeria flower corruption passage</meta>Greedy is his mouth. Insolent is his word in his rule, in the time of the breaking of bread = in the time of understanding: his throat. With the corners of his mouth he eats, behind his claws he takes his food; his mouth is neither wood nor stone. Great is his madness at Lahun Chan. As for his face where he sits: sinful is his face, sinful is his word, sinful is his speech, sinful is his understanding, sinful is his walk. Bandaged are his eyes where he sits; a red settlement is his mat. He sits in the midst of his rule, in the heap of his father, in the heap of his mother; nor does he know his mother. Quickly kindled is his heart by lust. Among the fatherless, those greedy for a father, among the motherless he shall walk; drunken is his spirit, lost is his understanding beside his father, beside his mother. There is no reverence in him, there is no goodness in his heart; only on the tip of his tongue is there a little boiling. He does not know how it shall come to an end, nor does he know what is at the end of his rule. That is when the time of his reign shall come to an end.

<note>A pen flourish marks the end of the paragraph.</note>

Here is Bolon ti ku: Bolon Chan, the face of the lordly men, he of the two-day mat, he of the two-day throne. This one came within the Ox Ahau katun, and there shall be another lord of the province <note>Maya: "peten", referring to the island or region of Yucatan</note>, the establisher of the word of another katun, when the word of the Ox Ahau katun shall come to an end in the time of the selling of sons. This shall be over the stammerers, the Itza: one bread of Chuen, one bread; there shall be ground up one single stone of the loincloth of the sin of the stammerers, the Itza. This is Bolon ti ku. This shall be the ending of the word of the Ox Ahau katun, and the coming of understanding to the rulership of the towns. At the ending of the word of the katun, then shall be made manifest the lineage of the noble-born, the <term>Batabob</term> <gloss>town governors</gloss>, and the other prudent men, and the lineage of the Batabob who had earth stamped secretly into their faces, when they were made as nothing by the mad sun, the mad katun.

<summary>This page continues the prophetic condemnation of corrupt rulers from the Chilam Balam of Chumayel, describing their greed, blindness, and loss of reverence before their reign ends. It then prophesies the close of the Ox Ahau katun under Bolon ti ku, foretelling the judgment of the Itza and the eventual restoration of the true lineage of the noble-born and town governors after a period of madness and humiliation.</summary>

The sages also worried that while the principle emerges through images and numbers, the verbal pronouncements of hexagrams and lines cannot encompass it entirely. Thus they once remarked by way of contrast, saying: "Spirit has no localized direction, and the *Changes* has no fixed physical form." They also said: "One yin and one yang is what is called the Way." 

Now, whatever has a localized direction and a physical form is a concrete object. Even Heaven and Earth, yin and yang, are concrete objects. Yet the function does not separate from concrete objects, and its efficacy transcends the realm of physical things. Therefore, that which subtly animates the ten thousand things without being fathomable is Spirit. It sets into motion thunder, wind, water, and fire, silently gathering the functions of movement, swaying, drying, and moistening. For this reason, the six children <note>the six derivative trigrams representing natural elements</note> are put to service under Qian and Kun <note>Heaven and Earth, the two primary hexagrams</note>. When the *Shuogua* <gloss>Discussion of the Trigrams</gloss> commentary speaks of subtly animating things, it does not include Heaven and Earth in the list of the six physical entities. 

Therefore, service takes the One as master, and considers Spirit to be the ultimate. CCXLIX

# Usury. i.

Nor does what I said regarding the purchase of money-rents stand in the way, for money is not a vendible thing, and that which is the medium of sale cannot be the object of it. For it must be known that just as we have movable and immovable goods in our possessions, so too do we have the right to both; this right itself can be sold just as the movables and immovables themselves. Therefore, it is not the money that is sold, but the right to receive those pecuniary rents. Once this is sold, the money itself passes over, just as the <term>ius patronatus</term> (right of patronage—the right of a patron to present a candidate for a church benefice), which cannot be sold, passes when the land that holds it is sold. 

Note, however, that if someone receives one hundred from Titius, so that Titius may establish for the debtor an annual rent of a greater quantity than he received, this is usury. For there is no rent to be purchased here unless Titius were a person who usually lets out his services for such an amount per year and sells them. Similarly, it seems to be usury when one demands more from a rent than the thing yields in fruits or profit. Note this well, for few pay attention to it. 

Observe also that such a contract, by which one buys the rents of possessions or a house, is commonly made under an <term>emphyteutic</term> (a long-term lease of land) or <term>libellary</term> (a contract based on a written deed or *libellus*) contract, with the agreement that the one who pays the pensions may repurchase them and free himself from said census. Hence, in some parts, it is called a "fictitious sale" or *terra chatba franchi*. And therefore, although a lease can be made for the price of the entire rent that a house or possession yields, it cannot be done so in this libellary contract. For such a person is bound to maintain it at his own expense (cf. *Codex* 4.66.2, *de iure emphyteutico*), and is bound to pay the pension even if the thing perishes by accidental cause, provided the greater part does not perish. It is otherwise for a simple tenant (*conductor*), for he is not bound to maintain it at his own expense (cf. *Digest* 19.2.25, *l. colonus*), nor is he bound if the thing perishes by chance without his fault (cf. *Decretals* 3.18.1, *c. propter sterilitatem*). 

Therefore, if one wants as much from the census as a simple tenant would pay, the contract is unjust and in fraud of usury because of the agreement to resell, concerning which see below § 76 and the following. And for this reason, regard should be had not to the fruits if they exceed, but to the quantity of money paid for the principal, such that this pension, multiplied by twenty years, ascends to the total valuation of the leased thing. Thus it was five per cent, as is the text in the *Authentica* *de non alienandis* § *quia vero* (in the *Authenticorum* *perpetua*, *Codex* 1.2.14), and there in the gloss, and Bartholomaeus follows this in the aforementioned law, as does the lord Bartholomaeus Cepola of Verona. And therefore, if one were to lease simply for profit, it could not be given by *libellum* except for five [percent]. Hence, because such a person is commonly burdened in the census, I judge such a contract to be commonly illicit and usurious by fraud.

<margin>45</margin>
¶ Whether one who buys grain in the blade, or wine in the vine, or oil and the like before they are ripe for less than they will be worth at the time they are ripe is a usurer, since it seems to be an interpreted loan (*mutuum interpretatum*): Baldus answers in *l. rica.* (*Codex* 4.32.15) that either the present payment is the cause of the seller's loss, and thus it is usury (per *c. in civitate*, *Decretals* 5.19.6); or it is merely a convention, because the payment is not made in the present, and thus the contract, though not usurious, is nevertheless illicit; or neither is the cause of loss, because the grain or wine is not worth more under such a quality due to the danger to which it is subject, and thus it is permitted (cf. *Digest* 18.1.8, *l. si finitas*). I understand this when it is bought not in general, but determinately, i.e., the grain of this field in the blade, or the wine of this vineyard, etc.

<margin>46</margin>
¶ Hold therefore for this entire eighth case, better understanding this rule: that if a loan is made principally with the hope of having something beyond the principal, no danger can excuse such a contract from being usury. But if the loan is made liberally and afterwards something is accepted because of the danger, it is excused.

<column-break/>

<margin>47</margin>
¶ The ninth case is by reason of administration: for example, if someone was bound to place the money of another in the purchase of estates, as a tutor, or in another profitable venture, and did not do so, the one whose money it is will be able to accept as much beyond the principal as he would likely have had in profit if he had placed it as he ought (cf. *Digest* 26.7.7, *l. tutor qui repto*). And this makes against prelates who can acquire for the church and do not (cf. *Decretum* 2.12.2.5).

<margin>48</margin>
¶ The tenth case is by reason of hostility. For whom I can pursue with the sword and despoil of goods, I can also lawfully extort usury from him (cf. *Decretum* 2.14.4.12). Provided there is no scandal to others.

<margin>49</margin>
¶ The eleventh case is by reason of ostentation. Example: I give you marked money for show, or even to be placed as a pledge, such that I want the very same money that I gave you to be restored to me in number, and something of profit beyond it. For such a contract is no longer a loan, but rather a lease, as in the gloss in *c. si feneraveris* (*Decretals* 5.19.6). And this is supported by *Digest* 13.6.3.1.

<margin>50</margin>
¶ The twelfth is by reason of a contract other than a true or interpreted loan. For usury consists only in a true or interpreted loan: when something is raised above the principal in a loan, because the use of the thing in a loan is not separated from the consumption of the loaned thing itself or its ownership. Therefore, one who raises something beyond the principal steals the use, and thus it is called usury; this is not so in other contracts. And when a contract appears and does not seem to be a loan, and yet is at least an interpreted one, I shall therefore subjoin many actions that are done in contracts different from an apparent loan.

<margin>51</margin>
¶ And first, concerning exchanges (*cambia*), it must be known that all are reduced to three: namely, real only, and secondly, real and by letters, and thirdly, dry.

<margin>52</margin>
¶ Concerning real exchange only: whether real exchange is permitted when some profit is accepted by reason of it. This is when someone has ducats in gold and wants coin, or having coin wants gold or another kind of money, and the money-changer (*capsore*) also wants something for the ducat. Is it usurious? I answer no, because there cannot be a loan in the money-changer in this. Hence, to diminish the principal cannot be usury, but to increase it well can be. This is noted in *Digest* 12.1.11. It could well be an injustice when excessive profit is accepted with respect to the labor. And although some say it is permitted only to money-changers who make a trade of this, and not to others, I do not see by reason of diversity why I cannot estimate the labor—now the reason of one ducat, one shilling, just like anyone else. However, it is true that those who make a trade of this can reasonably accept something more, because they bear greater labors since they are always prepared.

<margin>53</margin>
¶ Whether real exchange and by letters is permitted. It is done in two ways. First, in a good way: I have one hundred gold pieces here in Genoa and I would like them rendered to me in Rome. I agree with the money-changer that he should make me letters by which they give me ninety-five, and he profits from the remainder. Baldus answers in *c. 1, de plus peti.* that such a contract is licit and necessary, fortified by the law of nations and natural reason, in that the money-changer undergoes the dangers of the roads and the losses of messengers, the pensions of labors, and the salaries of agents (cf. *Digest* 14.2.1, *l. periculi*). Hence, if something is gained, it is just, provided industry is added to a licit thing. Yet, there could be injustice when one takes excessive profit in respect to labor, expenses, and risk, or when they provide "bad" (counterfeit or debased) money. The second type of exchange (*cambium*) is performed through letters and in reality in this way: There is a person from beyond the mountains who has one thousand Venetian ducats and, intending to carry them to Venice—where they are worth more—to spend them there, finds a money-changer (*campsor*) in his own country who has a branch of his exchange house in Venice. He hands the money over to him solely for the exchange to Venice, so that they may be returned to him in Venice. Such a contract can be licit; it occurs when one does not intend to gain profit by reason of the transfer, but rather brings it back for the sake of the country [of destination]. If, however, from the fact that he hands it over first beyond the mountains and receives it in Venice, he intends to have a profit, it will be usurious, since the prior transfer induces the rationale of a loan (*mutuum*) with the hope of having more than the principal. And thus, it will be usury.

¶ 4
¶ Whether "dry exchange" (*cambium siccum*) is licit: I answer that it is not. It is called "dry" because, in truth, it is dried up of charity, since it ruins the poor and dries up souls from the grace of God. It is performed in seven ways. First, in this manner: I receive in Florence from a money-changer ten pounds of *grossi* (a silver coin), which at that time are worth one hundred florins, with the pact that he must give to that same money-changer [the equivalent] within ten days after the contract is celebrated. The pounds of *grossi* in Venice are sometimes worth more, sometimes less. If he wishes to hold it from month to month, he renews it in the aforementioned manner. Such an exchange is illicit and a usurious contract, because there is a loan with the hope of having more than the principal. For although they are sometimes worth less, yet in most cases they are worth more, and one is not excused by reason of risk, as was shown above. The *Clarus* (a legal authority) holds this for those who have the eyes of the heart, in *d.c.fi. de usuris* <note>referring to the *Digest* or *Decretals* regarding usury</note>. Such a contract is to the ruin of cities, as experience—the mistress of all things—testifies. *c. § sit. de elec. li. vj.* <note>referring to the *Liber Sextus* of the Decretals</note>. And that it is illicit is commonly held by the doctors. 

Second, it is done in this way: I have here in Genoa 100 gold coins, and I hand them to Peter so that he may eventually make them answerable to me here in a month in Rome, where they are likely worth more, and it is believed so. This is likewise usurious, because it is a loan with the hope of having more than the principal (*c. consuluit* and *c. in civitate, de usura*). 

Third, it is done in this way: I have here in Genoa 100 gold coins, which you, Peter, need; you make them returnable to me from London or Bruges, here in three months, in a different kind of currency—for example, so many pounds sterling, and the like. This contract is commonly usurious according to Johannes and Goffredus, because it is commonly done so that one may profit from it. And although sometimes it might profit me, yet in estimation it holds a profit, and thus, since it is a loan with the hope of having more than the principal, it will be usury. Nor will the reason of risk excuse it, as has been said. The same is said when one existing in Genoa buys *turonenses* (Tours coins) to be received in France at such fairs, according to Alexander, *lo. cum*, since such things are bought for more or less according to the delay of time, and they intend the profit that commonly results. 

Fourth, it is done in this way: One existing in Genoa gives certain money to someone so that he may return it to him in crowns (*scuti*) in Lyon at the time of the fair that will take place there. For example, he estimates the crown here in Genoa at 28, and thus gives such money at the rate of 28 per crown, which will ascend to 100 crowns; these crowns in Lyon are for the most part worth 30, or at least more than 28. The same is said of [transfers] from here to Naples for so many *carlini* per ducat and the like, according to Monaldus; they are usurious (*alle. c. eiiciens. lxxxviij. di. et .d.c.fi. de usura*). 

Fifth, it is done thus: I am in need of money here in Genoa. I seek a loan and do not find one except on this pact: that I receive it at the rate of the exchanges of London or Bruges, although I, the receiver, do not have a bank in London or Bruges, nor does the lender. Therefore, he lends in this way because he wishes to carry his money from London, so that he may thus profit from such a contract from here in Genoa to London, and from London to Genoa. And thus it is clear that it is not permitted; whence he says that it is usury. 

<column-break/>

Sixth, it is done in the worst way, and it is called "re-exchange" (*recambium*). It is done in this way: I am in need of money here in Genoa; I seek someone who will lend me ten. There is someone who gives a loan at the rate of the exchanges of London, with the pact that he writes letters, and yet he does not send them if he retains them; and according to how he profits from the exchanges in going and returning, so he will take more than the principal, and he is a most wicked usurer. 

Seventh, exchange is done in the Roman Curia, which is a certain clear usury, even if it is cloaked under the guise of exchange. It is done thus: A cleric, having newly obtained some benefice, in need of money for the expedition of his bulls, asks a money-changer for a certain sum under a loan—for example, 100 ducats—to be restored in his homeland, for example in Tours, here in six months in the currency current there, to whomever the aforementioned money-changer shall appoint. The money-changer lends, but beyond the exchange arising from the variety of the value of money in different places, he exacts 5 or 8 per hundred. Such money-changers are undoubtedly usurers. 

And although some have attempted to defend that such dry exchange can be licitly done in the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth ways mentioned—by saying that it is not a contract of loan, but a permutation, or a purchase, or an unnamed contract, and that the profit arises by reason of doubt or of the country, and therefore it cannot be usury—yet against them is the text *d.c.fi.*, *a contrario sensu*, where it says: "He who gives 10 shillings so that at another time the same amount of grain, wine, or oil of that measure may be returned to him, which at that time are worth more—although he truly doubts whether they will be worth more or less at the time of payment—ought not to be reputed a usurer." There it is. Therefore, conversely, if they presumed they would likely be worth more at the time of payment, he would be a usurer. The contract exists, it seems, of purchase or permutation, or at least an unnamed contract, because he who gives money is to receive grain and the like; these are more distant from ducats and sterling. Therefore, hold undoubtedly that it is a contract of a loan interpreted with the hope of having more than the principal celebrated. Nor does it stand in the way that sometimes it is worth less, because for the most part, in estimation, he intends profit, and it is inherent. And according to Archidiaconus, *flo. in summa*, hold that such men are only "mental usurers," yet you should say they are also "real usurers," because they do not wish to give to the one seeking a loan except with this pact. And thus it is clear that they are mental and real usurers. Whence Hostiensis and Goffredus say such usurers are [usurers] however much they cloak themselves under the guise of permutation, purchase, or another contract, and they are more execrable than all others who make such contracts from fair to fair, since they exceed the hundredth [part], according to Hostiensis, with whom Alexander agrees. 

There is, however, a contract in which one should not call the contract usurious nor illicit, namely: There is someone who would like to go from Genoa to London for business; he would not like to carry money with him because of the risks. There will be someone to whom he gives his money here in Genoa, who makes the same amount answerable to him in London. But because, due to the abuse of the aforementioned merchants, he cannot know determinately how many pounds sterling his money is worth, he accepts letters of exchange from someone here in Genoa to whom he gave his money, and from that he profits something. I say that if this person does not give it here in order to profit from it through exchange, but only so that he may have his money in London, then such profit coming to him will not make him a usurer, since it comes to him rather by reason of uncertainty or of the country, which excuses from usury when the loan is not made with the hope of having more than the principal. If, however, he could know the price of his "dry" money and gave it thus, and wanted such letters of exchange, he would be a usurer, because he would now intend profit from the loan, nor would the uncertainty excuse him (*d.c.fi.*).

55 ¶ Utrum deponens pecuniam apud campisorem vel mercatores vel artifices pro qua quoniam negotiat det deponenti certum quid pro centenario licite recipiat? Respondeo secundum Baldum in lege .j. C. pro socio. aut talis deposuit in specie. et tunc quicquid illius est pecunia deposita tenet omne lucrum restituere deponenti. quia ex re illius locupletior factus est. arguitur lege qui usuras ff. de negotiis gestis. Sed ego non credo in conscientia quod teneatur de necessitate pro ea quae dixi Restitutio. de lucro quod usurarius percepit ex pecunia usuraria quod non tenetur restituere. Aut usus est licite. quia deposuerat in numero. et tunc si deponens non habuit animum fenerandi: et campisor liberaliter dat. vel ex quadam equitate: sic licite recipere potest sine usura. Si vero dat ex quadam necessitate credens se obligatum ex causa reponens quod dicit bona fides durat. scilicet credens quod liberaliter dedit. Mala obligatio antedictorum iusta parit receptionem per errorem soluti. l. si testamento. §. j. ff. de fideiussoribus. Si vero deponens habuit animum aliquid habendi lucri: sic usurarius est. quia verum mutuum est cum spe habendi ultra sortem: cum sit in numero non in specie: nisi depo fuisset ratione societatis cum periculo suo. sed quo ad restitutionem dic ut supra. Restitutio. j. in verbo usurarius.

56 ¶ Utrum deponens pecuniam dotalem apud mercatorem ita quod sit salva. et recipiat aliquid de lucro sit usurarius. vide. §. dos. §. xj. et societas. j. §. vij.

57 ¶ Circa contractum emptionis et venditionis. quae saepe intervenit mutuum verum vel interpretatum. Ideo plura quaeruntur.

58 ¶ Utrum mercator seu artifex sit usurarius qui illi qui statim solvit rem vendit pro minori precio quam illi qui non solvit in continenti: sed vult terminum: Respondeo. suppono primo quod dicit Scotus in .iiij. dist. xv. q. ij. et Ricardus in .iiij. q. xxiij. ar. iij. quod pensatio valoris rerum usualium non potest fieri a nobis nisi per coniecturalem seu probabilem opinionem. Et hoc quidem non punctualiter: sed sub quadam latitudine equitatis ut parvus excessus equitatem illam non corrumpit: sed tunc solum quando est ibi tantus excessus quod inequalitas clare videtur. Et talis excessus contractum viciosum reddit. Et hoc supposito respondeo ad questionem cum distinctione. quod aut talis venditor non excedit praefatam equitatis latitudinem cum illo qui vult terminum: ut pro mi, nori daret si statim solveret precium. et sic non est usura. Exemplum. estimat pretia talis panni ab aliquibus .x. ab aliis .xj. ab aliis .xij. statim solveti libenter daret .p. ix. vel .x. non solventi vult .xij. non est usura: cum non excedat ratione temporis equitatem latitudinis iusti precii. Si vero praefatam latitudinis equalitatem trascenderet. ut puta quod vellet .xiij. vel .xiiij. sic esset usura. ut consuluit. de usu. Idem dic de eo qui non vult prorogare terminum debitori nisi aliquo dato. v. c. consuluit.

59 ¶ Quid si ex inveterata mala consuetudine et paucitate pecunie currentis communiter vendit ad tempus plus quam invenire posset emptorem statim solventem: Respondeo Sanctus Thomas in quadam. q. et Gira. obdo. in suis contractibus. quod si tales solum hoc faciunt ut iustum precium extorqueant: non erunt usurarii. unde ne decipiaris: attende si precium occurrens sit iustum an non. Et hoc tibi demonstrare poterit si attendas an mercatores si venderent tali precio consideratis laboribus et ceteris: debitum lucrum communiter reportarent. quia si sic esset plus: non posset vendi sine usura. Si vero nullum lucrum communiter haberent: sic esset clarum quod non est iustum precium illud quod daret de presenti solventi. sed hoc proveniat potius ex nimia cupiditate pecunias habentium: qui tali precio volunt emere ut postea modo suo vendant. Et ideo si plus

<column-break/>

vendunt illo precio ad tempus: dummodo iustum precium non excedant quod deberet valere: si talis corruptela non esset non erit usura. quia nihil ultra debitum exigunt ratione temporis. Adverte etiam quod si quis esset in tali loco in quo communiter ementes non habent pecunias: sed emunt ad tempus possent vendere aliquid plus iusto precio occurrenti sine usura. # Usury. I.

55 ¶ Whether one who deposits money with a money-changer, merchant, or artisan—for the purpose of the latter trading with it—may lawfully receive a certain percentage from the depositor? I answer according to Baldus in law *j.*, *C. pro socio* (Code, On Partnership): either such a person deposited the money *in specie* (as a specific, identifiable sum), and in that case, whatever profit is made from that deposited money, he is bound to restore it all to the depositor, because he has become richer through the other’s property. This is argued in the law *qui usuras*, *ff. de negotiis gestis* (Digest, On Business Managed). However, I do not believe in conscience that he is necessarily bound to restore the profit that the usurer gained from the usurious money, for the reasons I stated under the heading *Restitution*. Or, he used it lawfully because he deposited it *in numero* (as a generic sum of money). In that case, if the depositor did not have the intention of lending at interest, and the money-changer gives a return out of generosity or a certain equity, then he may lawfully receive it without usury. But if he gives it out of a certain necessity, believing himself obligated, then the principle applies that "good faith endures"—that is, he believes he gave it freely. A faulty obligation of the aforementioned kind produces a just right to recover what was paid by mistake; *l. si testamento, §. j., ff. de fideiussoribus* (Digest, On Sureties). If, however, the depositor had the intention of gaining some profit, then he is a usurer, because this is a true loan (*mutuum*) with the hope of having something beyond the principal, since it is in number and not in species—unless the deposit was made by reason of a partnership (*societas*) at his own risk. But regarding restitution, see what was said above under *Restitution*, section 1, at the word "usurer."

56 ¶ Whether one who deposits a dowry with a merchant so that it may be safe, and receives some profit from it, is a usurer? See *§. dos* (dowry), *§. xj.*, and *societas* (partnership), *j. §. vij.*

57 ¶ Regarding the contract of buying and selling, in which a true or interpreted loan often intervenes, several questions arise.

58 ¶ Whether a merchant or artisan is a usurer if he sells an item to someone who pays immediately for a lower price than to someone who does not pay on the spot but desires a term of payment? I answer: I assume first what Scotus says in *IV, dist. 15, q. 2*, and Richard in *IV, q. 23, art. 3*, that the valuation of common goods cannot be determined by us except through a conjectural or probable opinion. And this is not done with mathematical precision, but within a certain latitude of equity, so that a small excess does not corrupt that equity; it only becomes corrupt when the excess is so great that the inequality is clearly seen. Such an excess renders the contract vicious. Assuming this, I answer the question with a distinction: either such a seller does not exceed the aforementioned latitude of equity with the one who wants a term—for instance, he would give it for less if he paid immediately—and thus it is not usury. Example: he estimates the price of such cloth at 10 by some, 11 by others, and 12 by others. If he would willingly give it for 9 or 10 to one paying immediately, but wants 12 from one who does not pay immediately, it is not usury, since it does not exceed the equity of the latitude of the just price by reason of time. If, however, he were to transcend the aforementioned equality of latitude—for example, if he wanted 13 or 14—that would be usury, as advised in *de usu*. Say the same of one who does not want to extend the term for a debtor unless something is given; *v. c. consuluit*.

59 ¶ What if, due to an inveterate bad custom and a scarcity of circulating currency, he commonly sells on credit for more than he could find a buyer paying immediately? I answer with Saint Thomas in a certain question, and Gira. obdo. in his *Contracts*: that if such people only do this to extort a just price, they will not be usurers. Therefore, so that you are not deceived, observe whether the current price is just or not. And this you can demonstrate if you observe whether merchants, if they were to sell at such a price, considering their labors and other factors, would commonly report a due profit. For if it were more than that, it could not be sold without usury. If, however, they would commonly have no profit, then it would be clear that the price given to one paying in the present is not the just price, but rather this arises from the excessive greed of those who have money, who want to buy at such a price so that they may later sell in their own way. And therefore, if they sell for more

<column-break/>

at a term, provided they do not exceed the just price that it ought to be worth if such corruption did not exist, it will not be usury, because they demand nothing beyond what is due by reason of time. Note also that if someone were in a place where buyers commonly do not have money, but buy on credit, they could sell for something more than the current just price without usury. The reason is that a merchant can value that merchandise more highly when he spends it later than when he spends it sooner. And therefore, if he sells for something more, only having regard to the profit they should reasonably report from such a negotiation, it will not be usury—not counting them as usurers if they only sell for so much more on credit that they report a moderate profit for the aforementioned labors, expenses, and other such things. However, he would not have this profit in the case of one who brings goods to a place where he believed he could sell much and profit due to their rarity, but because many others arrived, seeing that he would not yet report a profit—indeed, he would report a loss if he sold at the current price—he sells for more on credit so that he does not suffer a loss. This would be usury. For just as it is not permitted to lower the price if no others had arrived, so with the arrival of abundance, he cannot sell for more by reason of time. For in this case, he has with him the saying: "A thing is worth as much as it can be sold for" (*l. j. §. si be. res. ff. ad trebellianum*). But in the cases above, the truth is limited: that a thing is worth as much as it can be sold for, provided the aforementioned abuses do not stand in the way. And thus Thomas answers in *II-II, q. 77, ad 1*, where it is said: "The prices of things are determined not by the affection of individuals, but commonly." He says this is true, unless the affection is reasonable on the part of the seller, as it is in the two aforementioned cases, but not in this last one.

60 ¶ Whether one who sells an item to someone who needs money, so that he may immediately buy it back for a lower price, is a usurer? I answer that he is, because it is the same as if he were lending money. And this is the worst contract, which is called *stock and bistock* (a form of predatory double-dealing), because they commonly sell for more—and thus they strike with one sword—and afterwards buy back for less, and thus they impose another sword. If, however, someone had simply sold it for a just price without thinking of buying it back, and the buyer, not finding a buyer, wanted to sell it back to the seller for less, he would not be a usurer for buying it for less; but it could be an injustice, and it commonly happens in such a case, and therefore it is an illicit contract.

61 ¶ Whether one who sells an item on credit for more than it is worth by common estimation—but it is worth more either by its natural value, or because of the utility to the buyer, or because it was very useful to the seller, and demands a price according to that—is a usurer? I answer according to Scotus and Richard (where cited above) and Thomas (*II-II, q. 77*), that a thing cannot be estimated so that it is sold at such a price while maintaining justice. Not according to natural value, because then a fly would be worth more than all the gold in the world and all inanimate things. Nor according to the utility of the buyers, because then a medicinal herb or a potion that is worth an inestimable price to someone for their liberation from death would have to be sold at that price. But it must be estimated by common estimation, as has been said in the letter, *§*. And therefore, if it were sold for more than such an estimation by reason of time, it will be usury. If it is not by reason of time but for another respect, it will be an injustice, unless he sells to one who knows and is willing, as above, *Buying, §. 7*. However, it could well be estimated for more than the thing is worth by common estimation without usury by reason of one's own utility—for example, I have an item very useful to me, from which I profit much, and by its absence I will be much damaged; for that reason, it would be permitted

§. 11. The tenth reason: That which, without the intervention of any other, lies proximately next to the perfect and simple One, cannot be anything but one and simple. Because, if it were multiple and diverse, it would not be next to and similar to it; nor, because of the multiplicity and diversity contained within itself, could it be compared and assimilated with the indivisible One, nor be proximately united with it: since nothing is conjoined or proximately applied to the one except the one; just as a linear point is applied to a central point, and not a certain part of the line divided from it, and much less a surface or a body.

§. 12. The eleventh reason: Whatever order the first cause observes with its caused things, and by whatever fitting and convenient means it leads and promotes them to the ultimate end, which is its very essence, it is bound to observe the same, and to act in the same way with the perfect produced thing, which, without a doubt, is the first, and as close and near to the said end as is possible. But this cannot be done except by one degree only: because there is no diversity of degrees except according to how this or that is closer or further from its principle and its ultimate end. Whence it follows that that which is most near to it and immediately touches it—both by reason of unity and beginning, and by reason of end and perfection—is only one.
